--- title: "Seed Timing" subtitle: "When did the outbreak start? — smooth seeding, the (τ, λ) ridge, and reporting it honestly" draft: true execute: echo: true warning: false code-fold: true code-summary: "show code" --- "When did this outbreak start?" is a central question early on in an outbreak. The **seed time** τ is our answer to it — the moment local transmission was first established. But notice that a *time* only means anything relative to an origin: τ is not a calendar date, it is an *offset*, the number of days after some reference point t = 0 that we are free to choose. The origin is ours to set — the first observation, a vaccination campaign, a border closure, a policy change — and what inference actually recovers is the offset from it. (In the Washington example below we set t = 0 to 2020-01-21, so a posterior of τ ≈ 22 days reads as "the chain was seeded around 12 February.") Fixing the origin is what turns the vague "when did it start?" into an estimable number. And "the seed date" is really three questions of increasing difficulty: - **E1 — recover τ when the seed size is known.** The cleanest case; τ is identifiable. - **E2 — the origin / burn-in.** How much transmission preceded the first observation? - **E3 — the joint (τ, seed size).** The most honest, and the least identifiable: during exponential growth the data pin a *combination* of seed time and seed size, not either alone. This is the **seed-timing ridge** — the temporal twin of the initial-condition ridge in [Identifiability](identifiability.qmd), and the heart of this chapter. ## Real data: cryptic introduction in Washington State The early-2020 Washington State COVID-19 outbreak is the textbook cryptic-introduction case, and a good example dataset to show camdl's features for seed time and size inference. We now know from genomic analyses that the outbreak-clade common ancestor (tMRCA) is estimated to have emerged between **18 Jan and 9 Feb 2020** ([Bedford et al. 2020, *Science*](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abc0523)), weeks before the first observed community case (28 Feb). ::: {#cell-fig-covid .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Early-2020 WA daily reported cases (NYT). Index case 21 Jan (t=0, a travel import); ~5 near-flat weeks; explosion from late February. Red band = genomic clade-MRCA window (18 Jan–9 Feb); dashed line = first community case (28 Feb).](seed-timing_files/figure-html/fig-covid-output-1.png){#fig-covid width=1111 height=467} ::: ::: Here, for the sake of a teaching example, we assume we do not have genomic sequences or a tMRCA estimate, and ask: what can we learn about the seed time from statewide WA daily reported cases (NYT)? We fit the **pre-lockdown growth window, days 0–55**. Importantly, we drop the 21 Jan index case. This particular case was a lone travel import, and almost surely *not* the community-clade founder. In initial fits with this index case, a single smooth seed gives it ≈ 0 probability and a log-likelihood of −∞ (it's a worthwhile exercise to try to fit with this datapoint included). The seed-timing question is about the *cryptic* introduction, so we start with the first observed community case (28 Feb, t=38) as our day-0. The data before that are not just uninformative about the seed time, they are *misleading* --- they are noise from a separate process (travel import) that the model cannot represent. Additionally, WA interventions ramped 11–23 Mar, so a constant-β SIR cannot fit the lockdown-flattened tail. However, information about the seed timing lives in the early growth phase (e.g. pre-non-pharmaceutical interventions) regardless. Two structural choices in the model make the seed time inferable rather than assumed. The first is a smooth importation pulse, `seed rate = λ / (1 + e^−(t−τ)/w)`. The population starts fully susceptible (`S = N0`, `I = 0`), so transmission `βSI/N` is zero until something seeds the first cases — and the naïve fix, a hard initial condition `I(0) = seed`, would pin that seeding to t = 0, the very thing we want to infer. Letting infections instead arrive through an import that is ≈ 0 before τ and rises to a plateau λ over a fixed window w turns τ into the inflection point of the import curve: a free, continuous parameter. The onset is smooth rather than a step for two reasons — it keeps the likelihood continuous in τ (a step would flip a whole seeding event in or out as τ crosses a filter step), and it matches how cryptic introductions actually trickle in. λ trades off against τ, since a larger assumed seed pushes the inferred onset later; that trade-off is the seed-timing ridge, and it is why τ's posterior comes out broad rather than a spike. ::: {#cell-fig-pulse-shape .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The importation pulse. The seed rate is ≈ 0 before τ and rises to its plateau λ over a window of width w, with τ the inflection point. A hard step (dashed) would make the likelihood discontinuous in τ.](seed-timing_files/figure-html/fig-pulse-shape-output-1.png){#fig-pulse-shape width=736 height=242 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The second is a logistic reporting ramp, `ρ(t) = ρ_max / (1 + e^−(t−t_rep)/w_rep)`. We observe not infections but a fraction ρ of incidence, and early in an emerging outbreak that fraction is not constant: detection climbs from near-zero to a ceiling ρ_max as testing and case-finding scale up. Hold ρ fixed and the model can only bend the reported curve into the observed S-shape by speeding up β or shifting the seed — relabelling a surveillance artefact as epidemic dynamics and biasing the very τ and λ we are after. The ramp gives the reported fraction its own degree of freedom. We anchor t_rep to the known WA testing timeline rather than estimate it, because a later reporting onset and a later seed both delay the take-off and are confounded; whether the ramp earns its extra parameters we test directly in the model comparison below. ::: {#cell-fig-ramp-shape .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The reporting ramp (the same logistic form). The reported fraction climbs from ≈ 0 to a ceiling ρ_max around the onset t_rep over width w_rep, absorbing surveillance scale-up so it is not misread as transmission.](seed-timing_files/figure-html/fig-ramp-shape-output-1.png){#fig-ramp-shape width=734 height=242 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Model and parameters Six parameters estimated, four fixed. The free/fixed split is identical for both methods below (IF2 and PMMH); only the priors differ (IF2 ignores them). Priors are *general-coronavirus* — what one would have believed about an emerging coronavirus at the outbreak's start, **not** values back-fitted to SARS-CoV-2. | parameter | role | est/fixed | value or prior | rationale | |-----------|------------------------|-----------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `tau` | seed time (target) | **estimated** | `uniform(0, 45)` d | quantity of interest; flat prior lets the data speak | | `beta` | transmission rate | **estimated** | `log_normal(μ=−0.92, σ=0.4)`, median 0.40 | with γ prior, implied R₀ 90% CI ≈ [1.5, 5.5] | | `gamma` | recovery rate | **estimated** | `log_normal(μ=−1.97, σ=0.4)`, median 0.14 | infectious period ≈ 7 d (90% CI 3.7–14); **breaks the β/γ degeneracy** | | `lambda` | seed magnitude | **estimated** | `exponential(rate=0.5)`, mean 2 | non-identifiable from one growth curve; weak prior favours small cryptic seeds | | `rho_max` | ceiling reporting | **estimated** | `beta(2, 3)`, mean 0.40 | weakly informative | | `k` | NegBinomial dispersion | **estimated** | `log_normal(μ=3, σ=1)`, median 20 | weakly informative | | `N0` | initial susceptibles | fixed 1,000,000 | — | not identifiable on growth phase (S≈N ⇒ incidence ≈ βI, independent of N0); cumulative infections ≪ N0, so 1 M / 4 M / 7.7 M give the same likelihood | | `w` | seed-pulse width | fixed 5.0 d | — | a single smooth onset cannot resolve it | | `w_rep` | reporting-ramp width | fixed 7.0 d | — | surveillance scale-up timescale, ≈ 1 week | | `t_rep` | reporting-ramp onset | fixed 37.0 d | — | **external anchor**: known WA testing timeline (≈ first community detection) | Data are statewide WA (~7.7 M); early spread was concentrated in the Seattle / Puget Sound metro (~4 M). Because N0 is non-identifiable, this geographic ambiguity does not affect the seed-time estimate. `tau` and `t_rep` are `real`-typed; under IF2 their fit-bounds are not enforced (camdl#66), so the IF2 fits below set `transform = "logit"` as a workaround — the PMMH posterior sidesteps this entirely, since the prior defines τ's support. ## The likelihood landscape, interactively When fitting camdl models, especially tricky models with questionable identifiability, we recommend surveying the likelihood landscape first with `camdl survey`. Here, we do a 1800-point Latin-hypercube sweep with a particle-filter evaluation at each point (`camdl survey --fit fits/covid_wa_survey.toml --eval pfilter --render`), rendered as an interactive pair-plot. Pick any two parameters; the level-ridges that defeated the MLE show as diagonal high-likelihood bands (β–γ especially) rather than a single peak. A caveat for reading it: about 72% of the Latin-hypercube points land in low-likelihood regions where the particle-filter estimate is noisy (per-point SE > 1.7 nats), so the exact ranking of bad points is unreliable. However, the high-likelihood region — the ridge itself — is trustworthy (and as we'll see in a bit, its best point with loglik ≈ −78 matches the PMMH posterior mode with ≈ −77). The survey is a *diagnostic* that tells you the shape of the problem; the posterior above is the inference. ## Method 1 — Maximum likelihood (IF2) Next, we try a simple IF2 (iterated filtering) seeks the MLE by perturb-and-filter. On this data it **does not converge**: the level-setting parameters (λ, ρ_max, and the β/γ split) trade off along ridges, so there is no single peak to find. camdl's compound scout-convergence gate reports this directly — both legs fail across every IF2 configuration we ran: ::: {#cell-wa-if2-gate .cell execution_count=5} ::: {#wa-if2-gate .cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=5} | IF2 fit | worst-agreeing param (Â) | loglik spread Δ_dB | τ agreement Â | gate | |---|---|---|---|---| | all 6 free | rho_max (Â=9.890) | 124.5 dB | 1.000 | ✗ FAIL | | γ fixed at 0.14 | rho_max (Â=7.777) | 191.2 dB | 0.999 | ✗ FAIL | ::: ::: Both fail (threshold: Â ≤ 1.01, Δ_dB ≤ 30). The worst-agreeing parameter is always `rho_max` — the *level* of the curve, which trades off with λ and the β-magnitude along a flat ridge. Crucially, **fixing γ does not rescue it**: the β/γ growth-rate degeneracy is *not* the binding problem; the level ridge is. Only τ ever agrees across chains (Â ≈ 1.0). An optimiser cannot pin a valley — the remedy is not a better optimiser but the missing *information*, supplied as priors in a posterior. ### The fit calls, and what the gate actually prints The two scout runs are launched by `make if2` — identical 24-chain IF2 fits, one with all six parameters free and one pinning γ: ```bash # from this chapter's seed-timing/ directory; long-running, so run via `make if2` camdl fit run fits/covid_wa_if2.toml --seed 42 --stage scout --progress plain camdl fit run fits/covid_wa_if2_gammafix.toml --seed 42 --stage scout --progress plain ``` The table above is a digest of `camdl fit summary`. Its full output is more telling: the per-parameter Â column (note `rho_max` blowing past the threshold while `tau` sits at 1.000), the per-chain loglik-eval log-likelihoods and SEs that the decibans leg keys on, and the final compound verdict. Both are **FAIL**. Expand to see exactly what camdl reports: ::: {#wa-if2-summary-full .cell execution_count=6} ::: {#wa-if2-summary-full-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Method 2 — Bayesian posterior (PMMH) A posterior *explores* the ridge instead of failing to optimise on it. Two implementation facts: - **Priors regularise the ridge** (general-coronavirus, table above). The load-bearing prior is on γ (infectious period ≈ 1 week): the data fix `r = β − γ`, so an informed γ pins β. λ and ρ_max keep weak priors — their posteriors will reveal what the data add. - **PMMH, not PGAS.** PGAS's NUTS gradient does not yet cover the observation likelihood (camdl audit C1), so it cannot estimate ρ_max or k; PMMH is gradient-free and fine at *T* = 55. Sampler: 4 chains × 15 000 iterations, 800 particles (log-lik SD ≈ 0.12 nats), burn-in 3 000, thinned ×5, started at an interior point with finite prior density. **Convergence.** R̂, ESS, and the posterior summary: ::: {#cell-wa-posterior-table .cell execution_count=7} ::: {#wa-posterior-table .cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=7} | param | R̂ | ESS | posterior median | 90% CI | what the data say | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | τ (days) | 1.001 | 1371 | 22.42 | [6.71, 35.95] | **informed** (≈ Feb 12; far narrower than its flat prior) | | β | 1.000 | 1584 | 0.50 | [0.42, 0.61] | well determined | | γ | 1.001 | 1602 | 0.13 | [0.07, 0.24] | ≈ prior (growth phase can't split β/γ) | | λ | 1.000 | 1707 | 1.50 | [0.20, 6.27] | ≈ prior — **sloppy/non-identified** | | ρ_max | 1.000 | 1160 | 0.28 | [0.21, 0.47] | partially informed | | k | 1.000 | 1573 | 12.50 | [5.42, 27.29] | partially informed | ::: ::: All six R̂ = 1.00, ESS > 1000, acceptance ≈ 22% — converged, in contrast to the IF2 fits the gate rejects. Re-running the *same* sampler with the priors replaced by vague uniforms (≈ pure likelihood) makes it collapse the way IF2 does: acceptance falls, chains fail to mix, and the sloppy marginals balloon to the parameter bounds. ::: {#cell-wa-vague-vs-informative .cell execution_count=12} ::: {#wa-vague-vs-informative .cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=12} | param | informative R̂ | informative 90% CI | vague R̂ | vague 90% CI | |---|---|---|---|---| | tau | 1.00 | [6.71, 35.95] | 1.38 | [2.57, 43.75] | | beta | 1.00 | [0.42, 0.61] | 1.53 | [0.47, 5.00] | | gamma | 1.00 | [0.07, 0.24] | ✗ NaN | [1.00, 1.00] | | lambda | 1.00 | [0.20, 6.27] | 4.23 | [0.00, 100.00] | | rho_max | 1.00 | [0.21, 0.47] | 1.31 | [0.01, 1.00] | | k | 1.00 | [5.42, 27.29] | 1.00 | [0.10, 13.09] | ::: ::: With vague priors γ runs toward its bound, λ and ρ_max span their full ranges, and even τ loses its anchor — the same failure the IF2 gate reports. The general-coronavirus priors are what make the problem well-posed; they regularise the ridge, they do not dictate the answer. ## Was the reporting ramp necessary? Model comparison We added a logistic reporting ramp ρ(t) on the argument that early testing scaled up. Is it justified, or overfitting? We compare three PMMH models — constant ρ, ρ(t) ramp, and ρ(t) + process overdispersion — by prequential expected log predictive density (`camdl compare`, scored at each posterior mode). All three have the same estimated dimension, so the comparison is fair. ::: {#cell-wa-compare-table .cell execution_count=13} ::: {#wa-compare-table .cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=13} | Model | T_score | elpd | Δelpd | E_T | se(Δ) | evidence | crps | Δcrps | PIT_cov90 | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | constant rho | 55 | -79.17 | -2.06 | 0.127 | 2.72 | -9.0 dB, substantial against | 3.531 | +1.054 | 0.49 | | rho(t) + overdispersion | 55 | -77.17 | -0.06 | 0.940 | 1.20 | -0.3 dB, indeterminate | 2.639 | +0.161 | 0.56 | | rho(t) ramp | 55 | -77.11 | — | — | — | — | 2.478 | — | 0.53 | _Sorted by Δelpd ascending — best-supported model at the bottom._ ::: ::: The reporting ramp is **necessary**: dropping it (constant ρ) costs ΔELPD ≈ −2 with substantial evidence against, and a clearly worse CRPS. Process overdispersion is **unnecessary**: ΔELPD ≈ 0 (indeterminate) — once τ is estimated, extra process noise adds nothing. The posterior-predictive overlay shows why the constant-ρ model fits worse: it cannot bend its reported-case shape to reconcile a cryptic seed with a late detected onset. ::: {#cell-wa-compare-ppc .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Posterior-predictive medians (lines) with 50% bands for the constant-ρ model (blue) and the ρ(t)-ramp model (red), against observed reported cases (bars), days 0–55. The ρ(t) model tracks the delayed, accelerating onset; the constant-ρ model must compromise and sits above the early data and below the late climb.](seed-timing_files/figure-html/wa-compare-ppc-output-1.png){#wa-compare-ppc width=1156 height=496} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Two convergence verdicts, both honest"} The **MLE** fits never pass camdl's compound scout-convergence gate — the sloppy directions (λ everywhere, ρ_max with chain-agreement Â up to ≈ 14) keep the per-parameter agreement leg from clearing threshold. That is the *correct* verdict for a structurally sloppy model under optimisation: there is no single peak to agree on, only a ridge. The **posterior** does converge (R̂ = 1.00, ESS > 1000) because it does not chase a peak — it represents the ridge as a spread of jointly-plausible values, regularised by the priors. Same data, same model: an optimiser correctly fails, a sampler correctly succeeds. We never launder an MLE point estimate out of a gate that refuses; we report the posterior, which is honest about what the level-ridge leaves unknowable. ::: ## Reflections On synthetic data the seed time is recoverable when the seed size is known (E1), and the joint (τ, λ) problem is a genuine ridge (E3). On the WA data, an external anchor (the testing timeline pinning `t_rep`) plus general-coronavirus priors date the seed (τ ≈ 12 Feb, 90% CI ≈ [28 Jan, 26 Feb]) even though λ stays unknowable. The methodological point: on a model with a ridge, the optimiser correctly fails the convergence gate while the posterior converges and reports the ridge as a spread — same data, same model, two honest verdicts. --- ## Appendix — synthetic foundations The experiments below (run on synthetic data simulated from known parameters) establish the concepts the WA analysis rests on: the smooth seed, recovering τ when the seed size is known (E1), and the (τ, λ) ridge (E3). Kept here for reference. ## A smooth seed How do you make "introduction time" an estimable parameter? A discrete import event at τ is a step function in τ — its likelihood gradient is zero almost everywhere, so no gradient-based or iterated-filtering method can move it. The fix is a **smooth importation pulse**: a source-less inflow into `I` whose rate is a logistic soft-onset, $$ \text{seed}: \varnothing \to I \quad @ \quad \frac{\lambda}{1 + \exp\!\big(-(t - \tau)/w\big)}, $$ with τ the onset time, λ the importation strength (the **seed magnitude**), and `w` the pulse width — the timescale over which the influx ramps from ~0 to ~λ. Finite `w` makes the rate differentiable in τ, so every backend and sampler handles τ as an ordinary global parameter. `w` is the identifiability dial: small `w` gives sharp timing on a stiff surface; large `w` blurs τ into a slow ramp. The inflow has no infector, so the lineage layer mints each imported individual with `parent = Import` — the seed founders are Import-rooted in the transmission tree (see [Transmission Trees](../transmission-trees.qmd)). ::: {#cell-fig-seed-pulse .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6)) t = np.linspace(0, 80, 400) for tau, c in [(25, "#3366cc"), (40, "#d62728")]: ax1.plot(t, seed_rate(t, tau, TRUTH["lam"], TRUTH["w"]), color=c, lw=1.8, label=f"τ = {tau}") df = simulate_cases(f"/tmp/seed_tau{tau}.tsv", **{**TRUTH, "tau": tau}) ax2.plot(df["time"], df["cases"], color=c, lw=1.5, label=f"τ = {tau}") ax1.set_xlabel("time (days)"); ax1.set_ylabel("seed inflow rate"); ax1.legend(frameon=False) ax1.axvline(25, color="#3366cc", ls=":", lw=0.8); ax1.axvline(40, color="#d62728", ls=":", lw=0.8) ax2.set_xlabel("time (days)"); ax2.set_ylabel("daily cases"); ax2.legend(frameon=False) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: the logistic seed rate for two onset times τ (same λ, w) — a smooth, differentiable shift. Right: the resulting daily incidence (simulated) — a later seed simply translates the whole onset later, which is what makes τ recoverable when the seed size is fixed.](seed-timing_files/figure-html/fig-seed-pulse-output-1.png){#fig-seed-pulse width=1636 height=527} ::: ::: ## E1: recovering τ when the seed size is known We generate synthetic daily cases at **τ = 30** (β = 0.6, γ = 0.2, λ = 2.0, w = 3, N₀ = 5000, ρ = 0.5, k = 20) and ask the cleanest question: with every other parameter known, does the likelihood locate τ? Each point below is a particle-filter likelihood **slice** at the true nuisance values: ::: {#cell-fig-e1 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} taus = [12, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, 38, 42, 46] nuis = {k: v for k, v in TRUTH.items() if k != "tau"} lls = [pfilter_loglik(SYNTH, tau=t, **nuis) for t in taus] taus_f = [t for t, l in zip(taus, lls) if np.isfinite(l)] lls_f = [l for l in lls if np.isfinite(l)] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6)) ax.plot(taus_f, lls_f, "-o", color="#3366cc", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgewidth=1.3) ax.axvline(30, color=GREY, ls="--", lw=1) ax.annotate("truth τ = 30", (30, min(lls_f)), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, 4), fontsize=8, color=GREY) walls = [t for t, l in zip(taus, lls) if not np.isfinite(l)] if walls: ax.annotate(f"−∞ wall for τ ≥ {min(walls)}", (min(walls), np.median(lls_f)), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-4, 0), ha="right", fontsize=8, color="#d62728") ax.set_xlabel("seed time τ (days)"); ax.set_ylabel("log-likelihood") fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![1D likelihood slice over τ (all other parameters at their true values), synthetic data generated at τ = 30 (dashed line). The slice peaks at the truth and falls off smoothly; past the observed onset a seed *later* than the data cannot explain cases that have already happened, so the likelihood drops to −∞ (the wall, off-scale right). With the seed size known, τ is sharply identified.](seed-timing_files/figure-html/fig-e1-output-1.png){#fig-e1 width=1035 height=527} ::: ::: ## E3: the (τ, λ) ridge Now the honest question: estimate τ and the seed magnitude λ *together*. During exponential growth, $I(t) \approx N_{\text{seed}}\,e^{r(t-\tau)}$ with $N_{\text{seed}} \propto \lambda$, so the early case curve constrains the combination $\ln\lambda - r\tau$, not τ and λ separately: **a later seed with a larger influx produces a nearly identical early epidemic.** The likelihood is flat along that direction and steep across it — a sloppy ridge. ::: {#cell-fig-e3-ridge .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} taus = [22, 26, 30, 34, 38] lams = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0] nuis = {k: v for k, v in TRUTH.items() if k not in ("tau", "lam")} Z = np.array([[pfilter_loglik(SYNTH, tau=t, lam=l, **nuis) for l in lams] for t in taus]) Zm = np.where(np.isfinite(Z), Z, np.nan) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2)) im = ax.imshow(Zm, origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap="viridis", extent=[-0.5, len(lams) - 0.5, -0.5, len(taus) - 0.5]) ax.set_xticks(range(len(lams))); ax.set_xticklabels(lams) ax.set_yticks(range(len(taus))); ax.set_yticklabels(taus) ax.set_xlabel("seed magnitude λ"); ax.set_ylabel("seed time τ (days)") ax.scatter([lams.index(2.0)], [taus.index(30)], marker="*", s=180, color="white", edgecolors="black", zorder=3) fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="log-likelihood") fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![2D likelihood slice over (τ, λ) with β, γ, ρ, k at their true values. The high-likelihood band (yellow) runs **diagonally** — later seed times pair with larger seed magnitudes along ln λ ≈ rτ + const. The data cannot separate *when* from *how much*; it pins only the combination. The white star marks the true (τ=30, λ=2).](seed-timing_files/figure-html/fig-e3-ridge-output-1.png){#fig-e3-ridge width=963 height=617} ::: ::: The ridge is not a failure of the method — it is a true property of the data. The honest deliverable is the 2D surface itself, with the constrained combination $\ln\lambda - r\tau$ named, **not** a spuriously precise point estimate of τ. ## Does the ridge matter? Yes — and it doesn't break forecasting Three points along the ridge give very different (τ, λ) but near-identical case curves — which is exactly why the data can't separate them: ::: {#cell-fig-ridge-predictions .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} ridge = [(24, 0.7, "#2ca02c", "early-small (τ=24, λ=0.7)"), (30, 2.0, "#3366cc", "truth (τ=30, λ=2.0)"), (36, 5.5, "#d62728", "late-large (τ=36, λ=5.5)")] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8)) obs = pl.read_csv(SYNTH, separator="\t") ax.plot(obs["time"], obs["cases"], "o", ms=3, color=GREY, alpha=0.5, label="synthetic data") for tau, lam, c, lab in ridge: df = simulate_cases(f"/tmp/ridge_{tau}.tsv", **{**TRUTH, "tau": tau, "lam": lam}) ax.plot(df["time"], df["cases"], color=c, lw=1.6, label=lab) ax.set_xlim(0, 70); ax.set_xlabel("time (days)"); ax.set_ylabel("daily cases") ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=8) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Three points along the (τ, λ) ridge: an early-small seed, the truth, and a late-large seed. The simulated case curves are nearly indistinguishable through the growth phase — the data that would discriminate them does not exist. A model non-identifiable in (τ, λ) can still *forecast* the trajectory; identifiability and calibration are different things.](seed-timing_files/figure-html/fig-ridge-predictions-output-1.png){#fig-ridge-predictions width=1108 height=557} ::: :::
